confirmed: URL scheme: the month folder is 0-based and zero-padded; the day folder is 1-based and zero-padded. dukascopy-node v1.46.4 src/__mocks__/handlers.ts serves each mock at its exact datafeed URL (file.replace('src/__mocks__', 'https://datafeed.dukascopy.com/datafeed')). Folder 2019/01 holds 672 hourly records, which is 28 days, so February. New day-base test: each minute file matches the February hourly file 24/24 and its 2019 daily record only when the day folder is read as 1-based; read as 0-based it matches 0/24.

File names per timeframe match v1.46.4 src/url-generator/index.ts: BID_candles_min_1 per UTC day, BID_candles_hour_1 per month, BID_candles_day_1 per year, {HH}h_ticks per hour. There is no monthly 1m file.
Fixture provenance: all 5 local .bi5 files have git blob SHA-1s identical to the v1.46.4 tree, e.g. d586a094acaf55926b284d8e57b70ac2e6d18971 for EURUSD/2019/01/04/BID_candles_min_1.bi5.

LZMA-alone header: props 0x5D (lc=3, lp=0, pb=2), 4 MiB dictionary, known sizes 34,560 / 17,856 / 16,128 / 8,760. There is no end marker, and the decoder consumes each input to its last byte (5/5 files).

Record layout is 24-byte big-endian [int32 sec, open, close, low, high, float32 volume]. Three independent tests agree: (1) OHLC envelope, where only f3=low and f4=high pass; (2) open/close continuity, 689 and 682 of 1,439 pairs versus 93 and 101 reversed; (3) new test: the first flat of each zero-volume run equals the previous record's f2 in 60/60 runs and its f1 in 0/60. This matches v1.46.4 src/data-normaliser/index.ts 'const [sec, open, close, low, high, volume] = values;' and the decompressor's 5x readInt32BE + readFloatBE.

Time base: offsets are seconds from the UTC start of the file's bucket. The 2019 daily candles equal the hourly candles aggregated over UTC days, with flats removed, in 51/51 cases. Each minute file aggregates exactly to its hourly and daily candles.

Price scales in dukascopy-node v1.46.4 instrument-meta-data.json: eurusd 100000, gbpusd 100000, usdjpy 1000, xauusd 1000. EURUSD is verified on real data (1.14011-1.14603). Three-decimal Dukascopy gold is corroborated by a StrategyQuant forum report (https://strategyquant.com/forum/topic/gold-piptick-step-wrong-on-sq-x).

Closed periods are 'flats': all four prices equal the previous close and volume is 0. In winter 2019 they run Fri 22:00 to Sun 21:00 UTC (hour starts, inclusive). New Year's Day has no active hour until 22:00 UTC. The zero-volume days in the 2019 daily file are exactly the 52 Saturdays. The two weekday minute files contain no zero-volume minutes.

Node v25.2.1 has no built-in LZMA. zlib has gzip/deflate/brotli/zstd. DecompressionStream accepts gzip/deflate/deflate-raw/brotli; zstd, lzma and xz throw TypeError. Extra check: Windows' built-in tar.exe links liblzma but rejects a raw .bi5 ('Unrecognized archive format').

Prototype decoder: re-running test-lzma.mjs gives 152/152, all 400 bit flips throw, and decoding takes about 3.9 ms per file. My 70 extra decodes all pass: Python-liblzma vectors with a 4 KiB dictionary and data larger than it, nice_len 273 with BT4, HC3/BT2 match finders, and lc/lp/pb variants, each with unknown and known size. 3,000 fuzzed inputs all threw within 350 ms. Reviewing the code against LzmaSpec found no defect. The licence line 'LZMA SDK is placed in the public domain.' is on https://www.7-zip.org/sdk.html.

Volume arithmetic: 2020-01-01 to 2026-10-17 is 2,482 days (1,773 weekdays, 354 Sundays, 355 Saturdays) in 82 months. That is 9,928 requests, or 8,508 without Saturdays, and about 86 MB to download. Output reproduces at 44.5 B/row as JSON and 8.15-8.29 B/row gzipped, about 81 MB in total.

Upstream facts: #254 opened 2026-07-07 with the quoted 'TLS handshake completes ... never sends any response body' text, and the maintainer's 'dukascopy has changed the datafeed and underlying APIs' is accurate. The PR #257 tester wrote on 2026-07-17 'the old endpoint (datafeed.dukascopy.com) still times out'. v1.49.0 (2026-07-16) is the JSON-API engine rewrite; v1.50.0 (2026-07-24) removes decimalFactor. #261 (2026-10-17) reports HTTP 202, x-amzn-waf-action: challenge, server CloudFront, content-length 0, no Retry-After, failures from Node/urllib/curl/wget/curl_cffi, success only in headed Chrome, and retryCount 0 silently returning empty data. src/config/data-api.ts builds 'jetta' with String.fromCharCode(106,101,116,116,97), and jetta.dukascopy.com resolves to CloudFront.

dukascopy-node config docs (https://www.dukascopy-node.app/config/node): retryOnEmpty ('successful but empty (0 Bytes) responses should be retried'); ignoreFlats defaults to true (flats 'mainly come from non-trading days, such as weekends or bank holidays'); batchSize 10 and pauseBetweenBatchesMs 1000 ('Main purpose - not to fall under rate limiting restrictions'). The mock empty.bi5 is the 0-byte git blob e69de29b.

refuted.claim: The local TLS reset (and WebFetch's ECONNRESET) 'may not be local' and supports the access blocker: 'From this machine even the TLS handshake to *.dukascopy.com is reset ... So a plain Node script cannot rely on Dukascopy today.'
refuted.evidence: www.dukascopy.com is on Cloudflare (104.20.28.213 and 172.66.145.22 via 1.1.1.1). With curl --trace-time, the TCP connect to 172.66.145.22 took about 65 ms, yet the reset arrived 9 ms after the ClientHello ('ALPN: curl offers' at 19:27:58.622, 'Recv failure: Connection was reset' at 19:27:58.631). Control on the same Cloudflare network: https://nodejs.org (104.16.212.131, about 59 ms connect) completed its handshake and returned HTTP 200. A server about 60 ms away cannot answer in 9 ms, and Cloudflare does not reset handshakes for valid hostnames. The reset is therefore hostname (SNI) filtering on this network path: an ISP or national filter, or local security software. WebFetch fails identically. I found no published SPK/BTK decision naming Dukascopy (SPK routinely blocks foreign leveraged-FX sites, e.g. https://www.birgun.net/haber/spk-den-kaldiracli-doviz-islemi-yaptiran-42-siteye-erisim-engeli-459683). datafeed.dukascopy.com is a CNAME chain (datafeed.cloud.dukascopy.com, then datafeed.66proxymity88.net) whose answers alternate between AWS 16.62.187.25/16.62.244.190 and 194.8.15.180. My one GET resolved to 194.8.15.180 and timed out at TCP after 21 s. None of this measures how Dukascopy treats scripts.

issues.issue: The ACCESS blocker mixes up a filter on this machine's network with Dukascopy's policy, and it overstates #254 and #261 while leaving out contrary evidence. As written, the owner would believe scripts are universally blocked, and would not learn that nothing on *.dukascopy.com can be fetched from this network at all.
issues.fix: Restate ACCESS in three parts. (a) This network filters *.dukascopy.com by hostname, so no Dukascopy importer can run here. Choose the run location (CI runner or VPS) and test it, and do not bypass the filter, because its origin may be regulatory. (b) Upstream access is undocumented and unstable. In July the old feed failed for Node while curl results were mixed, and its status is unknown since 2026-07-17. The JSON API handled bulk scripted downloads in July, then returned 429s, and since 2026-10-16 at least one datacenter IP has received a WAF challenge on the tick endpoint. (c) Solving or replaying a WAF challenge is circumvention and stays off the table. The licence blocker remains decisive on its own.

issues.issue: The Terms-of-Use quotes are second-hand: search excerpts plus one data vendor's article. Neither the exact wording nor its scope is verified, including whether 'WEBSITE' covers datafeed.dukascopy.com.
issues.fix: Keep the conservative conclusion (written permission is needed for a shared archive shown to paying users), but label the quotes as unverified. The owner should open the live Terms of Use from a network where dukascopy.com loads, and ask Dukascopy in writing for a licence that covers automated download, storage and display to app users.

issues.issue: The suggested XAUUSD sanity band of 1,500-5,000 rejects valid prices from March 2020 and January-February 2026.
issues.fix: Check for scale errors instead of a narrow band. Compare each price with a broad per-symbol order-of-magnitude window (e.g. XAUUSD 300-30,000, USDJPY 50-500, EURUSD/GBPUSD 0.5-3). Separately, check continuity against the previous day's last close (e.g. flag moves over 20%).

issues.issue: Aggregating higher timeframes requires flats to be excluded, and the D1/H4 candle boundary needs a decision. If flats are kept, 9 of 51 daily candles come out wrong: every Sunday plus Jan 1 gets the stale Friday close as its open/low. Dukascopy's own daily candles start at 00:00 UTC (51/51 match).
issues.fix: Never store or synthesize flats, and have the browser aggregator treat missing minutes as 'no candle'. Decide explicitly whether the replay's D1/H4 candles start at 00:00 UTC, which gives a 2-3 h Sunday candle, or at the 17:00 New York roll.

issues.issue: Several facts are still unverified on real data: the GBPUSD, USDJPY and XAUUSD scales (metadata only), gold's daily break, the summer-time weekly open/close, and what a Saturday minute file contains. If the market-hours config is wrong, the gap report will be noisy.
issues.fix: Before any backfill, decode one known summer and one known winter weekday per symbol and check the scale and session times against the config. Until those checks pass, have the importer report 'unexpected flats' rather than fail the month.

issues.issue: Minor arithmetic and unit slips. 'Decoded about 327 MB' is 343 MB (327 MiB) for 9,928 files, or 294 MB without Saturdays. '1 request/s takes about 2.4 h' holds for 8,508 requests; 9,928 takes 2.76 h. '15-40 min' depends on whether the 250 ms gap is global, in which case the minimum is 35-41 min, or per worker.
issues.fix: State the units and which request count each duration assumes.

issues.issue: Rounding to per-symbol precision by multiplying (int * 1e-5) can produce float artifacts in the JSON.
issues.fix: Divide instead: int / 10**digits. All 11,520 values tested printed with 5 or fewer decimals that way.

issues.issue: The research reads intent into an implementation detail: it calls the char-code hostname in dukascopy-node a sign that automated bulk access is unwelcome. data-api.ts contains only the String.fromCharCode line, with no comment, so the motive is unknown.
issues.fix: Drop the inference, or label it as speculation.

report:
VERDICT: sound-with-fixes. The format work holds up under independent re-testing. The access narrative does not: it treats a filter on this machine's network as evidence about Dukascopy, and it stretches two GitHub reports beyond what they say. The terms quotes could not be verified first-hand. One concrete check (the gold price band) is wrong. The bottom line still stands: do not build the forex/gold archive on Dukascopy without Dukascopy's written permission. The licence issue alone justifies that.

WHAT HOLDS (re-derived independently):
- URL scheme. The month folder is 0-based: folder 2019/01 holds 672 hourly records, which is February. dukascopy-node's mocks are served at their exact datafeed URLs (src/__mocks__/handlers.ts). The day folder is 1-based; this was untested before. Each minute file matches its hourly and daily candles 24/24 under the 1-based reading and 0/24 under 0-based.
- Fixture provenance. All 5 fixtures have git blob SHA-1s identical to the v1.46.4 tree.
- Header. LZMA-alone, props 0x5D, 4 MiB dictionary, known size, no end marker, input fully consumed.
- Record layout. 24 bytes big-endian: [sec, open, close, low, high, float volume]. Three tests agree, including a new one: the first 'flat' of each closed run carries the previous record's field 2 (close) in 60/60 runs and field 1 in 0/60. A flat is a zero-volume record whose four prices all equal the previous close. This also matches the v1.46.4 normaliser and decompressor.
- Time base. Offsets count seconds from the UTC start of each file's period. Dukascopy's daily candles start at 00:00 UTC and equal the flat-free hourly aggregate in 51/51 cases. If flats are kept, 9 of 51 days come out wrong (every Sunday plus Jan 1), so stored and aggregated data must never contain flats.
- Scales from the library metadata: EURUSD/GBPUSD 100000, USDJPY/XAUUSD 1000. EURUSD is also verified on real data.
- Weekend and holiday behaviour matches the research (Fri 22:00 to Sun 21:00 UTC in winter; Saturdays fully flat).
- LZMA. Node 25 has no LZMA (verified), and Windows tar.exe cannot read a raw .bi5. The prototype decoder re-passes 152/152 tests, plus 70 extra decodes of my own (4 KiB dictionary, data larger than the dictionary, nice_len 273, lc/lp/pb variants) and 3,000 fuzzed inputs, all rejected within 350 ms. The LZMA SDK's public-domain statement is verified.
- Volume. The arithmetic and the 44.5 / 8.2 B-per-row output figures reproduce.

WHAT IS WRONG:
1. The local failure is not Dukascopy's doing. www.dukascopy.com sits on Cloudflare. Its handshake is reset 9 ms after the ClientHello, although the round trip is about 65 ms, while nodejs.org on the same Cloudflare network connects normally. That pattern means a filter on this network path (ISP, national filter or local security software) is blocking by hostname. Separately, datafeed.dukascopy.com currently resolves to either AWS addresses or 194.8.15.180. My single allowed GET (XAUUSD 2025-07-17) went to 194.8.15.180 and timed out at TCP, and nothing was downloaded. Consequences: no Dukascopy importer can run from this network, and the run location has to be chosen and tested.
2. #261 is narrower than reported: one reporter plus one 'same issue' comment, the tick endpoint only, from a datacenter VPS, with no test from a residential network or VPN. The research also leaves out PR #257, where on 2026-07-17 a script downloaded the full XAUUSD m1 history through the JSON API (about 17,000 requests, zero failures).
3. #254 also contains 'curl and wget still download the same files without any problem'. The last data point on the old feed is 2026-07-17, so its current status is unknown rather than dead.
4. The research says an exact-phrase search confirmed the terms wording. My exact-phrase searches found no Dukascopy page. The only corroboration is a data vendor's article, so the quotes are unverified (not disproven).
5. The suggested 1,500-5,000 gold sanity band rejects real prices: about $1,451 in March 2020 and about $5,300-5,590 in January 2026.

FIXES: see issues and corrections. Rewrite the access blocker in three parts (local filter; unstable, undocumented upstream; no WAF circumvention). Mark the terms quotes as unverified. Replace the gold band with an order-of-magnitude plus continuity check. Exclude flats before aggregating, and decide where D1/H4 candles start. Before any backfill, check each symbol's scale and session times on real data.
